title: Black Grapes and Their Places
description: The principal black grapes, the regions that made them famous and how place changes the wine.
L: Describe Cabernet in Bordeaux's Left Bank

Cabernet Sauvignon is a cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc, born in Bordeaux in the 17th century. On the gravel soils of the Médoc, which drain well and store heat, it leads the blend in wines like Pauillac and Margaux. The style: blackcurrant, cedar, high tannin and acidity, built to age.

Cabernet buds and ripens late. In cool years it can keep a green pepper note, from pyrazines that only break down with full ripeness. That's why it needs warm, well-drained sites. Warm regions like Napa Valley give riper blackcurrant, softer tannins and 14.5% alcohol or more.
Why does Cabernet Sauvignon thrive on the gravel of the Médoc?
Gravel drains and stores heat, helping a late ripener
Gravel warms the roots and drains water, both helping a late-ripening grape in a moderate climate.

Napa Valley made Cabernet famous in the New World after the Judgment of Paris in 1976. Chile's Maipo gives ripe blackcurrant with a minty note. Australia's Coonawarra, on red terra rossa soil, gives eucalyptus and mint; Margaret River gives an elegant, Bordeaux-like style.
Match each region to its Cabernet character.
Cabernet keeps its blackcurrant core while place changes the rest.
Cabernet leads the blends of Bordeaux's gravelly Left Bank
As a late ripener it needs warmth, or it tastes green
Napa, Maipo, Coonawarra and Margaret River each give a distinct style
Describe Merlot on Bordeaux's Right Bank

Merlot is the most planted grape in Bordeaux. On the Right Bank, in Pomerol and Saint-Émilion, it leads the blend. Clay and limestone soils hold water and stay cool, suiting an early-ripening grape. The wines show plum, black cherry and a velvety texture; Pétrus, in Pomerol, is almost pure Merlot.

Merlot buds and ripens about one to two weeks before Cabernet Sauvignon. That lets it ripen on cool clay where Cabernet would struggle. But early budding brings frost risk, and its thin skin makes it sensitive to rot. In warm places it can overripen fast, losing freshness and turning jammy.
Merlot ripens later than Cabernet Sauvignon.
Not true. Merlot ripens one to two weeks earlier, which is why it suits cooler clay soils.

Merlot is grown widely: in Italy, notably in Tuscany's Bolgheri and in Friuli; in Chile and California for soft, fruity reds; in Washington State for structured, fresh versions; and in New Zealand's Hawke's Bay. The 2004 film Sideways hurt its reputation in the United States, though great Merlot never went away.
Which wine is famous for being made almost entirely from Merlot?
Pétrus, in Pomerol, is almost pure Merlot. Margaux is Cabernet-led; Sassicaia is Cabernet-based; Vega Sicilia is Tempranillo-led.
Merlot leads the Right Bank blends of Pomerol and Saint-Émilion
It ripens early, suiting cool clay soils
It's grown widely, from Italy to Washington and New Zealand
Name its key New World regions
Explain why Pinot needs a cool climate

Pinot Noir is Burgundy's red grape. On the Côte d'Or's limestone and marl slopes, it gives wines that can be light in colour yet intense in aroma: red cherry, raspberry, and with age, earth, game and forest floor. Gevrey-Chambertin, Vosne-Romanée and Pommard are famous villages.

Pinot's thin skins and early ripening make it fragile. In heat, it ripens too fast, losing its delicate aromas and acidity, and turns jammy. In cool places, the long, slow season builds complexity. It is also prone to rot, frost and virus, and mutates easily; Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc are colour mutations of it.
Thin skins, early ripening, cool sites
Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc are colour ____ of Pinot Noir.
They arose as natural mutations of the skin colour. Genetically, they are almost identical to Pinot Noir.

Pinot thrives in Oregon's Willamette Valley, California's Sonoma Coast and Santa Barbara, New Zealand's Central Otago and Martinborough, Germany, where it's called Spätburgunder, and in Champagne as part of the blend. Each gives a different balance of fruit, earth and spice.
Which region is NOT a well-known home of Pinot Noir?
The Barossa is hot and best known for Shiraz. The others are cool regions famous for Pinot Noir.
Burgundy's Côte d'Or is Pinot Noir's benchmark
Thin skins and early ripening need a cool climate
Oregon, Sonoma, Central Otago and Germany grow fine Pinot
Compare Syrah in the Rhône and Australia

In the northern Rhône, Syrah grows on steep granite slopes in Côte-Rôtie and Hermitage, giving firm, peppery, blackberry wines. In Australia it's Shiraz, the country's most planted grape. The Barossa makes ripe, full wines with chocolate and spice; cooler sites, like the Yarra or Canberra, give peppery styles closer to the Rhône.
Rhône: pepper. Barossa: chocolate and ripe fruit.

Grenache, from Spain, where it's called Garnacha, loves heat and drought. Its thin skins give paler wines with red fruit, spice and high alcohol, often 15%. Grown as bush vines on poor soils, it can live over 100 years. It is the main grape of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Priorat and many rosés, and part of sweet fortified wines like Banyuls.
Grenache: heat, red fruit, high alcohol
Thin skins, red fruit and high alcohol
Grenache has thin skins and reaches high sugar levels. It's paler than Syrah but strong in alcohol.

Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre, often called GSM, are blended across the southern Rhône and in Australia. Grenache brings red fruit and alcohol, Syrah brings colour and structure, Mourvèdre brings tannin, meaty notes and dark fruit. Châteauneuf-du-Pape allows 13 varieties, but most wines are led by Grenache.
Match each grape to what it brings to a GSM blend.
Each grape fills a gap in the blend. Viognier belongs to the northern Rhône, co-fermented with Syrah.
Syrah is peppery in the Rhône and riper as Barossa Shiraz
Grenache gives red fruit, spice and high alcohol, and loves heat
GSM blends combine Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre
Describe Tempranillo in Rioja and Ribera

Tempranillo is Spain's leading red grape, early-ripening, as its name, from temprano, suggests. In Rioja it is often blended with Garnacha and aged in oak, traditionally American, giving vanilla, coconut and red fruit. In Ribera del Duero, high on the plateau, it's called Tinto Fino and gives darker, more powerful wines. In Portugal it's Tinta Roriz or Aragonez.

Sangiovese is Italy's most planted red. Its thin skins and high acidity give medium colour, firm tannin, sour cherry, tomato leaf and dried herbs. It's the grape of Chianti and Chianti Classico, of Brunello di Montalcino, which must be 100% Sangiovese, and of Vino Nobile di Montepulciano. Its acidity makes it great with tomato-based food.
Sangiovese: sour cherry and high acidity
Match each wine to its description.
Tempranillo leads in Spain; Sangiovese in central Italy.
When you taste a red with sour cherry and tea-like tannin that makes you crave pasta with tomato sauce, think Sangiovese. If it smells of vanilla, leather and strawberry, think Rioja.
Brunello di Montalcino must be made entirely from Sangiovese.
Yes. Brunello di Montalcino is 100% Sangiovese by law, unlike Chianti, which can include other grapes.
Tempranillo leads Rioja and Ribera del Duero, often with oak
Sangiovese gives Chianti and Brunello their sour cherry and acidity
Both have regional names and long ageing traditions
Describe Nebbiolo in Barolo and Barbaresco
Describe Malbec in Cahors and Mendoza

Nebbiolo, from Piedmont, is pale in colour but very high in tannin and acidity, with aromas of rose, tar, cherry and dried herbs. It ripens very late, often in October, in the fog, or nebbia, that may give it its name. Barolo and Barbaresco are its great wines, and both need long ageing to soften.
Pale colour, huge tannin, rose and tar

Malbec comes from south-west France, where Cahors makes dark, tannic wines once called black wine. In Argentina's Mendoza, at 800 to 1,500 m, it found new life. Strong sun and cool nights give deep purple colour, ripe plum and violet, and softer tannins. Argentina now grows more Malbec than anywhere else in the world.
Why is a Barolo pale in colour yet very tannic?
Nebbiolo has few colour pigments but lots of tannin
It's aged in white wine barrels
Nebbiolo's skins are low in stable colour pigments yet rich in tannin. Colour isn't a good guide to its power.

Every 100 m of altitude cools the air by about 0.6 degrees. In high vineyards like Valle de Uco, at up to 1,500 m, nights are cool, so grapes keep acidity. The intense ultraviolet light thickens skins, adding colour and tannin. That's why Mendoza Malbec is ripe and dark yet fresh.
High altitude: cool nights, intense light
Match each grape to its key region.
Nebbiolo stays at home in Piedmont; Malbec has an Old World home in Cahors and a New World one in Mendoza.
Nebbiolo is pale but very tannic, and makes Barolo and Barbaresco
Malbec comes from Cahors and found fame in Mendoza
Altitude gives Mendoza Malbec colour and freshness
Five grapes that complete the map
Name a classic region for each

Zinfandel, the same grape as Italy's Primitivo, came from Croatia and became California's heritage red, with ripe bramble fruit and high alcohol, often from old vines in Lodi and Sonoma. Pinotage is South Africa's own cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsault, made in 1925, giving dark, smoky wines with red fruit.

Gamay is the grape of Beaujolais, light and fruity, often with carbonic maceration. Carmenère, once grown in Bordeaux, was nearly lost there after phylloxera. In 1994 it was found in Chile, where it had been mistaken for Merlot. It gives dark fruit and a green, peppery note when not fully ripe.
Carmenère was found in Chile in 1994
Match each grape to its country of fame.
Each grape is closely tied to one country's identity.

Touriga Nacional is Portugal's finest red grape, giving dark, floral wines in the Douro and Dão, and a key grape in Port. Tannat, from south-west France, has very high tannin; Uruguay adopted it as its national grape. Its name is close to the word tannin, and with good reason.
Carmenère was rediscovered in Chile after being mistaken for Merlot.
Yes. In 1994, DNA analysis and ampelography showed many Chilean Merlot vineyards were actually Carmenère.
Zinfandel is California's heritage red; Pinotage is South Africa's own
Gamay makes Beaujolais; Carmenère is Chile's rediscovered grape
Touriga Nacional leads in Portugal; Tannat in Uruguay

Link each grape to its classic regions
Explain how climate and soil shape each
Match each grape to its classic region.
Each grape has a benchmark place.
Which grape is pale in colour yet very tannic?
Nebbiolo has few stable pigments but lots of tannin and acidity.
Which grapes are part of a classic GSM blend?
GSM stands for Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre.
Merlot ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon.
Yes. That's why Merlot suits the cooler clay of the Right Bank.
In Spain's Ribera del Duero, Tempranillo is called Tinto ____.
Tinto Fino is the local name. Tinta Roriz is the Douro's name, and Tinto Cão is a different Portuguese grape.
Cabernet and Merlot shape Bordeaux's two banks
Pinot Noir and Nebbiolo need special sites and time
Syrah, Grenache, Tempranillo and Sangiovese lead their regions
Malbec, Zinfandel, Pinotage and Carmenère define New World countries
